decks.title: Matrices — Part 1: Order, types, equality, addition and subtraction
goals: State the order of a matrix and classify it as a row, column, square, zero or identity matrix
Use equality of matrices to find unknown elements
Decide when two matrices can be added and add or subtract them
Multiply a matrix by a rational number and solve equations such as 2A + X = B

slides.heading: Matrices, Part 1
slides.body_md: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns.

visual.alt: Table of plates sold at an imagined school canteen: on Monday 30 idli and 18 dosa, on Tuesday 25 idli and 22 dosa. Written as a matrix with one row per day and one column per dish, it has 2 rows and 2 columns.
visual.caption: The same numbers as a matrix: $\begin{bmatrix} 30 & 18 \\ 25 & 22 \end{bmatrix}$, order $2 \times 2$.

slides.narration: Welcome to matrices. A matrix is simply numbers arranged in rows and columns, like a small table. Here an imagined school canteen records the plates of idli and dosa sold on two days. Keeping the numbers in their places lets us add, compare and multiply whole tables at once.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Recognise **row, column, square, zero** and **identity** matrices
Use **equality of matrices** to find unknowns
Solve equations such as $2A + X = B$
slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. You will name the order and type of a matrix, use equal matrices to find unknown numbers, decide when matrices can be added, and add, subtract and multiply them by numbers. Finally you will solve simple matrix equations.

slides.heading: Rows, columns and elements
slides.body_md: Each number in a matrix is an **element**. The element in row $i$ and column $j$ is written $a_{ij}$: row first, then column. Matrices are named with capital letters and written inside square brackets.

visual.alt: Table naming the elements of the matrix with rows 3, minus 5 and 0, 8: the element a one one in row 1 and column 1 is 3; a one two is minus 5; a two one is 0; a two two is 8. The first number in the name is the row, the second the column.
visual.caption: Element positions in $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -5 \\ 0 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$: row first, then column.

slides.narration: Each number in a matrix is called an element. We name an element by its row and then its column. In this matrix, the element in row one and column two is minus five, and the element in row two and column one is zero. Always say the row first.

slides.heading: The order of a matrix
slides.body_md: A matrix with $m$ rows and $n$ columns has **order** $m \times n$ (read "$m$ by $n$") and $mn$ elements.

visual.alt: Table of four matrices and their orders: a matrix with one row of three numbers has order 1 by 3; a matrix with one column of two numbers has order 2 by 1; a matrix with two rows and two columns has order 2 by 2; a matrix with two rows of three numbers has order 2 by 3.
visual.caption: Order $=$ rows $\times$ columns, always rows first.

slides.narration: The order of a matrix tells its size: the number of rows, then the number of columns. A matrix with two rows and three columns has order two by three and six elements. Do not swap the numbers: two by three and three by two are different orders.

slides.heading: Quick check: order
slides.body_md: Rows first, then columns.
slides.narration: Count the rows, then the columns, and write them in that order.

slides.heading: Types of matrix
slides.body_md: A matrix is named by its shape and by its elements.

rows: square; $1$ on the leading diagonal, $0$ elsewhere

visual.alt: Table of types of matrix: a row matrix has only one row, for example 3 and minus 2; a column matrix has only one column, for example 5 over 1; a square matrix has as many rows as columns; a zero or null matrix has every element 0; the identity matrix is square with 1 on the leading diagonal and 0 elsewhere.
visual.caption: Five types of matrix used in this chapter.

slides.narration: A row matrix has only one row and a column matrix only one column. A square matrix has as many rows as columns. In a zero, or null, matrix every element is zero. The identity matrix is square, with one on the leading diagonal, from top left to bottom right, and zero everywhere else.

slides.heading: Naming a matrix
slides.body_md: Shape first, then the elements.

nodes.label: Count the rows and the columns
$1$ on the leading diagonal, $0$ elsewhere: **identity matrix**

visual.alt: Flow chart for naming a matrix: count the rows and columns. One row gives a row matrix; one column gives a column matrix; equal numbers of rows and columns give a square matrix, and a square matrix with 1 on the leading diagonal and 0 elsewhere is the identity matrix. A matrix whose elements are all 0 is a zero matrix of any order.
visual.caption: Naming a matrix by its shape and its elements.

slides.narration: To name a matrix, first count its rows and columns. One row means a row matrix, one column a column matrix, and equal numbers of rows and columns a square matrix. Then look at the elements: all zeros give a zero matrix, and a square matrix with ones on the leading diagonal and zeros elsewhere is the identity.

slides.heading: Quick check: square or identity?
slides.body_md: Look at the leading diagonal and the other elements.
slides.narration: Is every square matrix an identity matrix? Think of a square matrix with other numbers in it.

slides.heading: Equality of matrices
slides.body_md: Two matrices are **equal** when they have the **same order** and **every pair of corresponding elements is equal**.

rows: same order, same element in every position
same order, but the elements in two positions differ

visual.alt: Table of three pairs of matrices: the first pair is equal because the orders and all elements match; the second pair holds the same numbers 2 and 5 but one is a row and the other a column, so they are not equal; in the third pair the orders match but the elements in two positions differ, so they are not equal.
visual.caption: Equal matrices: same order and equal corresponding elements.

slides.narration: Two matrices are equal only when they have the same order and the elements in matching positions are equal. A row holding two and five is not equal to a column holding two and five, because the orders differ. Equality gives one equation for each position.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: unknowns from equal matrices
slides.body_md: Find $x$ and $y$ if $\begin{bmatrix} x + y & -2 \\ 6 & x - y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 11 & -2 \\ 6 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.

visual.alt: Graph of the two straight lines x plus y equals 11, falling from left to right, and x minus y equals 3, rising from left to right. They cross at the point (7, 4), so x equals 7 and y equals 4 satisfy both equations.
visual.caption: The two equations from equal elements meet at $(7, 4)$.

slides.narration: The matrices have the same order, so we equate corresponding elements. Row one column one gives x plus y equals eleven. Row two column two gives x minus y equals three. Adding the two equations, two x is fourteen, so x is seven, and then y is four. The graph shows the two lines meeting at seven, four.

slides.heading: Quick check: equal matrices
slides.body_md: Equate the elements in the same position.
slides.narration: Match the element containing b with the element in the same position on the other side.

slides.heading: Adding and subtracting matrices
slides.body_md: Matrices of the **same order** are added (or subtracted) by adding (or subtracting) **corresponding elements**. Matrices of different orders cannot be added.

nodes.label: Do $A$ and $B$ have the same order?
Add or subtract corresponding elements; the result has the same order
$A + B$ and $A - B$ are not defined

visual.alt: Flow chart for adding or subtracting matrices: first ask whether A and B have the same order. If yes, add or subtract the elements in corresponding positions, and the answer has the same order. If no, the sum and the difference are not defined.
visual.caption: Compatibility for addition and subtraction.

slides.narration: Before adding, check the orders. If two matrices have the same order, add the elements in matching positions; the answer has that same order. Subtraction works in the same way. If the orders differ, the sum is simply not defined.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: sum and difference
slides.body_md: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -3 \\ 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 5 \\ 3 & -6 \end{bmatrix}$, find $A + B$ and $A - B$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Both are $2 \times 2$, so both answers are defined.

visual.alt: Working table for A equal to the matrix with rows 4, minus 3 and 0, 7 and B with rows minus 2, 5 and 3, minus 6: adding corresponding elements gives rows 2, 2 and 3, 1; subtracting gives rows 6, minus 8 and minus 3, 13.
visual.caption: Add or subtract position by position; watch the signs.

slides.narration: Both matrices are two by two, so we may add and subtract. Work position by position. Four plus minus two is two, and minus three plus five is two. For the difference, take care with signs: minus three minus five is minus eight, and seven minus minus six is thirteen.

slides.heading: Matrices as data
slides.body_md: Adding matrices adds whole tables of data in one step.

visual.alt: Table of books issued by an imagined school library: Class 9 borrowed 12 and then 10 fiction books, 22 in all, and 9 and then 6 non-fiction books, 15 in all; Class 10 borrowed 7 and 11 fiction books, 18 in all, and 15 and 8 non-fiction books, 23 in all.
visual.caption: Adding the two weekly matrices: $\begin{bmatrix} 12 & 9 \\ 7 & 15 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 6 \\ 11 & 8 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 22 & 15 \\ 18 & 23 \end{bmatrix}$.

slides.narration: Matrices are useful for data. An imagined school library records the fiction and non fiction books borrowed by two classes in each of two weeks. Adding the two weekly matrices gives the totals for both weeks in one step, position by position.

slides.heading: Multiplying by a number
slides.body_md: For a number $k$ (an integer or any non-zero rational number), $kA$ is found by multiplying **every element** of $A$ by $k$. The zero matrix $O$ and the negative $-A$ behave like $0$ and $-a$.

rows: $k$ may be any non-zero rational number

visual.alt: Table of rules: to find k times A multiply every element by k, so 3 times the matrix with rows 2, minus 1 and 0, 4 has rows 6, minus 3 and 0, 12; k may be a fraction such as one half; adding the zero matrix changes nothing; adding minus A to A gives the zero matrix.
visual.caption: Scalar multiples, the zero matrix and the negative of a matrix.

slides.narration: To multiply a matrix by a number, multiply every element by that number. The number can be a fraction, such as one half. Adding the zero matrix changes nothing, and adding the negative of a matrix gives the zero matrix, just as with ordinary numbers.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: combining scalar multiples
slides.body_md: If $P = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ and $Q = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -6 \\ 2 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$, find $3P - \dfrac{1}{2}Q$.

visual.alt: Working table: 3 P has rows 6, 0 and minus 3, 9; one half of Q has rows 2, minus 3 and 1, 4; subtracting element by element gives rows 4, 3 and minus 4, 5.
visual.caption: Scalar multiples first, then subtract.

slides.narration: First find each scalar multiple. Three times P multiplies every element by three. Half of Q halves every element. Then subtract position by position. For example, six minus two is four, and zero minus minus three is three.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a matrix equation
slides.body_md: Solve $2A + X = B$ for $X$, where $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 1 \\ -2 & 10 \end{bmatrix}$.

visual.alt: Working table for 2A plus X equals B: make X the subject, X equals B minus 2A; 2A has rows 8, minus 4 and 2, 6; subtracting from B gives X with rows minus 3, 5 and minus 4, 4; adding 2A and X gives back B.
visual.caption: Treat the matrix equation like a linear equation.

slides.narration: Treat the matrix equation like a linear equation. Subtract two A from both sides, so X equals B minus two A. Double every element of A, then subtract from B position by position. Finally check: two A plus X gives back B.

slides.heading: Quick check: one element of a combination
slides.body_md: You only need one position.
slides.narration: Pick out the elements in row one, column two, and combine just those.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Order $m \times n$: rows first, then columns
Types: row, column, square, zero (null), identity
Equal matrices: same order, equal corresponding elements
Add or subtract only matrices of the same order
$kA$: multiply every element by $k$; solve $2A + X = B$ like a linear equation

rows: same order and equal corresponding elements
only for the same order; work element by element

visual.alt: Summary table for part 1: order is rows by columns; the types are row, column, square, zero and identity; equal matrices have the same order and equal corresponding elements; only matrices of the same order can be added or subtracted; k times A multiplies every element by k; matrix equations are solved like linear equations.
visual.caption: Part 1 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. The order of a matrix is rows by columns. Matrices are named row, column, square, zero or identity. Equal matrices have the same order and equal corresponding elements. Only matrices of the same order can be added or subtracted, and a scalar multiple multiplies every element.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Finding unknowns (3 marks):** equations from equal elements 1 + each value 1
**Matrix equation (3 marks):** rearranged 1 + scalar multiple 1 + answer 1
**Mistake:** writing the order as columns by rows
**Mistake:** multiplying only one row by the number
slides.narration: Write the equations from equal elements before solving them, because each one earns a mark. In a matrix equation, rearrange first, then compute. Most lost marks come from signs, so write a bracket around every negative number you subtract. And remember: a number multiplies every element.

decks.title: Matrices — Part 2: Multiplication of matrices
goals: Decide whether two matrices can be multiplied and state the order of the product
Multiply a 2 × 2 matrix by a 2 × 2 or 2 × 1 matrix, and a 1 × 2 matrix by a 2 × 2 matrix
Show with an example that AB ≠ BA, and use AI = IA = A
Find unknowns from matrix products and work with A²

slides.heading: Matrices, Part 2
slides.body_md: Multiplying matrices: rows of the first by columns of the second.

nodes.label: Columns of $A$ $=$ rows of $B$: $AB$ is defined

visual.alt: Flow chart for multiplying matrices: A has order m by n and B has order n by p. When the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B, the product A times B is defined, and it has order m by p.
visual.caption: Compatibility for multiplication.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Multiplying matrices is not done position by position. Instead, each row of the first matrix meets each column of the second. First we learn when a product is defined and what its order is, then how to work it out.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Check **compatibility** for multiplication and state the order of a product
Show that $AB \ne BA$ in general, and use $AI = IA = A$
Work out $A^2$ and expressions such as $A^2 - 3A + 5I$
slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. You will check whether a product is defined, multiply using the row by column rule, and see why the order of multiplication matters. You will also use the identity matrix, find unknowns from a product, and simplify expressions with A squared.

slides.heading: When is a product defined?
slides.body_md: $AB$ is defined only when the **number of columns of $A$ equals the number of rows of $B$**. If $A$ is $m \times n$ and $B$ is $n \times p$, then $AB$ is $m \times p$.

visual.alt: Table of orders: 2 by 2 times 2 by 2 is defined and gives 2 by 2; 2 by 2 times 2 by 1 gives 2 by 1; 1 by 2 times 2 by 2 gives 1 by 2; but 2 by 1 times 2 by 2, and 2 by 2 times 1 by 2, are not defined because the inner numbers differ.
visual.caption: Inner numbers must match; the outer numbers give the order.

slides.narration: Write the two orders side by side. If the inner numbers match, the product is defined, and the outer numbers give its order. A two by two matrix times a two by one matrix gives a two by one matrix. But a two by one matrix times a two by two matrix is not defined.

slides.heading: Quick check: order of a product
slides.body_md: Inner numbers match? Outer numbers give the order.
slides.narration: Write the orders two by two and two by one side by side, then read off the outer numbers.

slides.heading: The row-by-column rule
slides.body_md: The element in row $i$ and column $j$ of $AB$ is found by multiplying the elements of **row $i$ of $A$** by the corresponding elements of **column $j$ of $B$** and adding.

visual.alt: Table of the row by column rule for A with rows a, b and c, d and B with rows p, q and r, s: the element in row 1 column 1 of A times B is a p plus b r; row 1 column 2 is a q plus b s; row 2 column 1 is c p plus d r; row 2 column 2 is c q plus d s.
visual.caption: Each element of $AB$: a row of $A$ times a column of $B$.

slides.narration: To find one element of the product, take a row of the first matrix and a column of the second. Multiply first with first and second with second, then add. Row one with column one gives the top left element, row one with column two the top right, and so on.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a stall's takings
slides.body_md: An imagined juice stall sells small cups at ₹30 and large cups at ₹50. It sells $40$ small and $25$ large on Saturday, and $55$ small and $30$ large on Sunday. Find $SP$ for $S = \begin{bmatrix} 40 & 25 \\ 55 & 30 \end{bmatrix}$ and $P = \begin{bmatrix} 30 \\ 50 \end{bmatrix}$.

visual.alt: Working table for an imagined juice stall: on Saturday 40 small cups at 30 rupees and 25 large cups at 50 rupees give 2450 rupees; on Sunday 55 small and 30 large cups give 3150 rupees.
visual.caption: Each row of $SP$ is one day's takings.

slides.narration: Check the orders first: two by two times two by one gives a two by one matrix, one row for each day. Saturday's row times the price column gives forty times thirty plus twenty five times fifty, which is two thousand four hundred and fifty rupees. Sunday gives three thousand one hundred and fifty rupees.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: multiplying in both orders
slides.body_md: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$, find $AB$ and $BA$.

visual.alt: Working table for A with rows 3, minus 1 and 2, 4 and B with rows 0, 2 and 1, minus 3: A times B has rows minus 1, 9 and 4, minus 8, while B times A has rows 4, 8 and minus 3, minus 13. The two products are different.
visual.caption: Same two matrices, different products.

slides.narration: For A times B, row one of A, three and minus one, meets column one of B, zero and one, giving minus one. Continue for the other three positions. Then multiply the other way round, B times A. The answers are completely different, so the order of multiplication matters.

slides.heading: Quick check: one element of a product
slides.body_md: Row 1 of the first, column 2 of the second.
slides.narration: Use row one of the first matrix and column two of the second: multiply in pairs and add.

slides.heading: Order matters: AB and BA
slides.body_md: Matrix multiplication is **not commutative**: in general $AB \ne BA$. Sometimes only one of the two products is even defined.

visual.alt: Table comparing the products from the worked example position by position: row 1 column 1 is minus 1 in A times B but 4 in B times A; row 1 column 2 is 9 against 8; row 2 column 1 is 4 against minus 3; row 2 column 2 is minus 8 against minus 13. No position agrees.
visual.caption: In general $AB \ne BA$: the order of the factors matters.

slides.narration: Compare the two products from the worked example position by position. Not a single element agrees. So with matrices we must always keep the order of the factors. Sometimes only one order is defined at all, as with a two by two matrix and a column matrix.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: One counter-example is enough.
slides.narration: Decide whether A times B always equals B times A. Remember the worked example.

slides.heading: The identity matrix
slides.body_md: For every square matrix $A$ of order $2$, $AI = IA = A$, where $I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

visual.alt: Working table for A with rows 5, minus 2 and 3, 7: multiplying by the identity matrix on the right or on the left gives A back, because every product with 0 vanishes and every product with 1 keeps the element.
visual.caption: $AI = IA = A$: the identity matrix acts like the number $1$.

slides.narration: The identity matrix behaves like the number one. Multiply any two by two matrix by the identity, on the left or on the right, and you get the same matrix back. The zeros remove the unwanted products and the ones keep each element.

slides.heading: A product can be zero
slides.body_md: For matrices, $AB = O$ does **not** mean $A = O$ or $B = O$.

visual.alt: Working table for A with rows 1, minus 1 and minus 2, 2 and B with rows 3, 1 and 3, 1: every element of A times B is 0, so A times B is the zero matrix although neither A nor B is zero; B times A has rows 1, minus 1 and 1, minus 1.
visual.caption: Two non-zero matrices with $AB = O$.

slides.narration: With numbers, if a product is zero then one factor must be zero. Not so with matrices. Here neither A nor B is the zero matrix, yet A times B is the zero matrix. And B times A is not zero, another reminder that order matters.

slides.heading: Algebra that changes for matrices
slides.body_md: Keep $AB$ and $BA$ apart when you expand.

rows: $AB = O$ is possible with $A \ne O$ and $B \ne O$

visual.alt: Table comparing numbers with matrices: numbers commute but matrices in general do not; a product of numbers is zero only if a factor is zero, but two non-zero matrices can multiply to the zero matrix; the square of a sum of matrices is A squared plus A B plus B A plus B squared; the identity matrix behaves like the number 1.
visual.caption: Rules from algebra that change for matrices.

slides.narration: Some rules of algebra change for matrices. Matrices do not commute in general. A product can be zero with neither factor zero. So the square of A plus B is A squared plus A B plus B A plus B squared, not A squared plus two A B plus B squared. The identity still acts like one.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: an expression in A squared
slides.body_md: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, show that $A^2 - 3A + 5I = O$.
bullets: **Step 3 —** Combine position by position: every element is $0$, so the result is $O$.

visual.alt: Working table for A with rows 2, 3 and minus 1, 1: A squared has rows 1, 9 and minus 3, minus 2; 3A has rows 6, 9 and minus 3, 3; 5I has 5 on the leading diagonal; combining position by position gives the zero matrix.
visual.caption: Square first, then combine element by element.

slides.narration: A squared means A times A, using the row by column rule, not squaring each element. Then find three A and five I. Combine the three matrices position by position. Every element comes to zero, so the expression is the zero matrix.

slides.heading: Quick check: a square
slides.body_md: Row by column, not element by element.
slides.narration: Multiply the matrix by itself using rows and columns; do not square each element.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: unknowns from a product
slides.body_md: Find $x$ and $y$ if $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 11 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}$.
bullets: **Step 2 —** Double the first and add the second: $7x = 21$, so $x = 3$.

visual.alt: Graph of the lines 3x plus y equals 11, falling steeply, and x minus 2y equals minus 1, rising gently. They cross at the point (3, 2), so x equals 3 and y equals 2 is the solution of the matrix equation.
visual.caption: The two equations from the product meet at $(3, 2)$.

slides.narration: Multiply out the left side: the top row gives three x plus y, and the bottom row gives x minus two y. Equate these with eleven and minus one. Doubling the first equation and adding the second, seven x is twenty one, so x is three, and then y is two. The two lines on the graph meet at three, two.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: $AB$ is defined when columns of $A$ $=$ rows of $B$; $(m \times n)(n \times p)$ gives $m \times p$
$AB \ne BA$ in general; $AB = O$ is possible with $A, B \ne O$
$A^2 = A \times A$; find unknowns by multiplying out and equating

rows: $AB$ needs columns of $A$ $=$ rows of $B$; order $m \times p$
element $(i, j)$ of $AB$ $=$ row $i$ of $A$ times column $j$ of $B$
$AB = O$ does not force $A = O$ or $B = O$
$A^2 = A \times A$, not the square of each element

visual.alt: Summary table for part 2: A times B needs the columns of A to equal the rows of B; each element is a row of A times a column of B; A times B and B times A usually differ; the identity leaves a matrix unchanged; a product can be zero without either factor being zero; A squared is A times A, not the square of each element.
visual.caption: Part 2 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up part two. A product is defined when the columns of the first equal the rows of the second. Each element is a row times a column. The order of multiplication matters, a product can be zero without zero factors, and the identity leaves a matrix unchanged. A squared means A times A.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Product (2–3 marks):** working shown 1 + each correct row or element 1
**Mistake:** multiplying corresponding elements instead of rows by columns
**Mistake:** assuming $AB = BA$, or expanding $(A + B)^2$ as $A^2 + 2AB + B^2$
**Mistake:** forgetting to check the orders first
slides.narration: Show the row by column working for at least one element, because method marks depend on it. Check the orders before you multiply, and state the order of the answer. Never assume that A times B equals B times A. And A squared is A times A, never the square of each element.

notes.title: Matrices — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Matrices and their order
sections.body_md:
A **matrix** is a rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns, written inside square brackets and named with a capital letter. Each number is an **element**; $a_{ij}$ is the element in row $i$ and column $j$.

- A matrix with $m$ rows and $n$ columns has **order** $m \times n$ (rows first) and $mn$ elements.
- $\begin{bmatrix} 6 & -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ has order $1 \times 3$; $\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix}$ has order $2 \times 1$; $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ -3 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$ has order $2 \times 2$.

*Example:* a canteen's sales over two days, with one row per day and one column per dish, form a $2 \times 2$ matrix.

key_terms.definition_md: A rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns.
One number in a matrix; $a_{ij}$ is in row $i$, column $j$.

visual.alt: Table of four matrices and their orders: a matrix with one row of three numbers has order 1 by 3; a matrix with one column of two numbers has order 2 by 1; a matrix with two rows and two columns has order 2 by 2; a matrix with two rows of three numbers has order 2 by 3.
visual.caption: Order $=$ rows $\times$ columns, always rows first.

visuals.alt: Table naming the elements of the matrix with rows 3, minus 5 and 0, 8: the element a one one in row 1 and column 1 is 3; a one two is minus 5; a two one is 0; a two two is 8. The first number in the name is the row, the second the column.
visuals.caption: Element positions in $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -5 \\ 0 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$: row first, then column.

visuals.alt: Table of plates sold at an imagined school canteen: on Monday 30 idli and 18 dosa, on Tuesday 25 idli and 22 dosa. Written as a matrix with one row per day and one column per dish, it has 2 rows and 2 columns.
visuals.caption: The same numbers as a matrix: $\begin{bmatrix} 30 & 18 \\ 25 & 22 \end{bmatrix}$, order $2 \times 2$.

sections.heading: 2. Types of matrices
sections.body_md:
- **Row matrix:** only one row, e.g. $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$.
- **Column matrix:** only one column, e.g. $\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$.
- **Square matrix:** as many rows as columns, e.g. order $2 \times 2$.
- **Zero (null) matrix** $O$: every element is $0$ (any order).
- **Identity matrix** $I$: a square matrix with $1$ on the leading diagonal (top left to bottom right) and $0$ elsewhere; of order $2$ it is $I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

Every identity matrix is square, but a square matrix need not be an identity matrix.

key_terms.definition_md: A matrix with only one row (order $1 \times n$).
A matrix with only one column (order $m \times 1$).
A matrix with as many rows as columns.
A matrix whose elements are all $0$, written $O$.
A square matrix with $1$ on the leading diagonal and $0$ elsewhere, written $I$.

sections.heading: 3. Equality of matrices
sections.body_md:
Two matrices are **equal** when they have the **same order** and **equal corresponding elements**. Equality gives one equation for each position, which is how unknowns are found.

*Example:* $\begin{bmatrix} x + y & -2 \\ 6 & x - y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 11 & -2 \\ 6 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ gives $x + y = 11$ and $x - y = 3$, so $x = 7$ and $y = 4$.

$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$ hold the same numbers but are **not** equal: their orders differ.

key_terms.definition_md: Matrices of the same order whose corresponding elements are equal.
Elements in the same row and column of two matrices of the same order.

visual.caption: One equation for each position that holds an unknown.

sections.heading: 4. Compatibility for addition and multiplication
sections.body_md:
- **Addition and subtraction:** $A + B$ and $A - B$ are defined only when $A$ and $B$ have the **same order**; the result has that order.
- **Multiplication:** $AB$ is defined only when the **number of columns of $A$ equals the number of rows of $B$**. If $A$ is $m \times n$ and $B$ is $n \times p$, then $AB$ is $m \times p$.

*Examples:* a $2 \times 2$ matrix times a $2 \times 1$ matrix gives a $2 \times 1$ matrix; a $1 \times 2$ matrix times a $2 \times 2$ matrix gives a $1 \times 2$ matrix; a $2 \times 1$ matrix times a $2 \times 2$ matrix is not defined.

key_terms.definition_md: Two matrices of the same order.
$AB$ is defined when columns of $A$ $=$ rows of $B$.

sections.heading: 5. Addition, subtraction and multiplication by a number
sections.body_md:
- **Sum and difference:** add or subtract corresponding elements: $\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -3 \\ 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 5 \\ 3 & -6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.
- **Scalar multiple:** for a number $k$ (an integer or a non-zero rational number), $kA$ multiplies **every** element by $k$: $\dfrac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} 8 & -2 \\ 6 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.
- $A + B = B + A$, $A + O = A$, $A + (-A) = O$.
- **Matrix equations** are solved like linear equations: $2A + X = B$ gives $X = B - 2A$; $\dfrac{1}{2}X + A = B$ gives $X = 2(B - A)$.

key_terms.definition_md: $kA$: every element of $A$ multiplied by the number $k$.
$-A$: every element of $A$ with its sign changed; $A + (-A) = O$.

sections.heading: 6. Multiplying matrices
sections.body_md:
**Row-by-column rule:** the element in row $i$ and column $j$ of $AB$ is row $i$ of $A$ times column $j$ of $B$ (multiply in pairs and add):

$\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} p & q \\ r & s \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} ap + br & aq + bs \\ cp + dr & cq + ds \end{bmatrix}$, and $\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} p \\ r \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} ap + br \\ cp + dr \end{bmatrix}$.

*Example:* $\begin{bmatrix} 40 & 25 \\ 55 & 30 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 30 \\ 50 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2450 \\ 3150 \end{bmatrix}$ gives a stall's takings for two days.

**Unknowns from a product:** multiply out and equate: $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 11 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}$ gives $3x + y = 11$ and $x - 2y = -1$, so $x = 3$, $y = 2$.

key_terms.definition_md: Each element of $AB$ is a row of $A$ times a column of $B$.

visual.alt: Table of the row by column rule for A with rows a, b and c, d and B with rows p, q and r, s: the element in row 1 column 1 of A times B is a p plus b r; row 1 column 2 is a q plus b s; row 2 column 1 is c p plus d r; row 2 column 2 is c q plus d s.

sections.heading: 7. Properties of matrix multiplication
sections.body_md:
- **Not commutative:** in general $AB \ne BA$ (and one of them may not even be defined).
- **Identity:** $AI = IA = A$ for every square matrix $A$ of order $2$.
- **Zero products:** $AB = O$ is possible with $A \ne O$ and $B \ne O$.
- **Squares:** $A^2 = A \times A$ (row by column, not the square of each element), and $(A + B)^2 = A^2 + AB + BA + B^2$.

*Example:* for $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, $A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 9 \\ -3 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$ and $A^2 - 3A + 5I = O$.

*Not in the ICSE 2027 syllabus:* adding, subtracting or multiplying matrices of order larger than $2 \times 2$; in this chapter all such working stays within order $2 \times 2$.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Order, type and equality (1–2 marks):* order rows by columns 1; each unknown 1.
- *Sums, differences and matrix equations (2–3 marks):* rearranged 1; scalar multiple 1; answer 1.
- *Products (2–4 marks):* orders checked and working shown 1; each correct row or element 1.
- *"Show that" with $A^2$ (3–4 marks):* $A^2$ 1–2; other terms 1; conclusion 1.
- *10-mark structured question:* parts (a), (b), (c) usually 3 + 3 + 4; show all working.

**Common mistakes**
1. Writing the order as columns by rows.
2. Adding matrices of different orders, or multiplying when columns of the first $\ne$ rows of the second.
3. Multiplying corresponding elements instead of rows by columns.
4. Squaring each element to find $A^2$.
5. Assuming $AB = BA$, or that $AB = O$ forces $A = O$ or $B = O$.
6. Sign slips when subtracting negative elements.

questions.stem_md: A matrix has $3$ rows and $2$ columns. What is its order?
questions.solution_md: The order is written as (number of rows) by (number of columns), so it is $3 \times 2$. Option (b) swaps rows and columns, (c) is the number of elements and (d) adds the rows and columns.

questions.stem_md: What kind of matrix is $\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & -7 \end{bmatrix}$, and what is its order?
questions.solution_md: It has one row and three columns, so it is a row matrix of order $1 \times 3$. The order always gives the rows first.

questions.stem_md: Pick the identity matrix of order $2$: the matrix that leaves every square matrix of order $2$ unchanged when it multiplies it.
questions.solution_md: The identity matrix has $1$ in each place of the leading diagonal (top left to bottom right) and $0$ everywhere else. Option (d) has its $1$s on the other diagonal, and (b) has a $0$ on the leading diagonal.

questions.stem_md: If $\begin{bmatrix} x + 3 & 5 \\ -1 & 2y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 5 \\ -1 & -6 \end{bmatrix}$, what is the value of $x + y$?
questions.solution_md: Equal matrices have equal corresponding elements: $x + 3 = 7$ gives $x = 4$, and $2y = -6$ gives $y = -3$. So $x + y = 4 + (-3) = 1$. Option (a) uses $y = 3$, and (b) forgets to halve $-6$.

questions.stem_md: Matrix addition needs matching orders. In which pair below can the two matrices be added?
questions.solution_md: Only (a) has two matrices of the same order, $2 \times 1$ and $2 \times 1$. The other pairs have orders $1 \times 2$ and $2 \times 1$, $2 \times 2$ and $2 \times 1$, and $1 \times 2$ and $2 \times 2$.

questions.stem_md: If $A$ is a $2 \times 2$ matrix and $B$ is a $2 \times 1$ matrix, the product $AB$ is
questions.solution_md: $AB$ is defined because $A$ has $2$ columns and $B$ has $2$ rows. The product takes the rows of $A$ and the columns of $B$, so its order is $2 \times 1$.

questions.stem_md: $P$ is a column matrix of order $2 \times 1$ and $Q$ is a square matrix of order $2 \times 2$. Which of the products $PQ$ and $QP$ can be found?
questions.solution_md: For $PQ$, $P$ has $1$ column but $Q$ has $2$ rows, so $PQ$ is not defined. For $QP$, $Q$ has $2$ columns and $P$ has $2$ rows, so $QP$ is defined, of order $2 \times 1$.

questions.stem_md: Given $A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -2 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ -3 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$, find $A + B$.
questions.solution_md: Add corresponding elements: $A + B = \begin{bmatrix} 5 + 1 & -2 + 4 \\ 3 + (-3) & 0 + 6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 2 \\ 0 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$. Option (a) is $A - B$, (b) is $B - A$ and (c) multiplies corresponding elements.

questions.stem_md: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -6 \\ 2 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$, which matrix is $\dfrac{3}{2}A$?
questions.solution_md: Multiply every element by $\dfrac{3}{2}$: for example $\dfrac{3}{2} \times 4 = 6$ and $\dfrac{3}{2} \times (-6) = -9$. Option (b) is $\dfrac{1}{2}A$, (c) is $3A$, and (d) multiplies only the first row.

questions.stem_md: Find the matrix $X$ for which $2X + A = B$, where $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 9 \\ -1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$.
questions.solution_md: $2X = B - A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 10 \\ -6 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, so $X = \dfrac{1}{2}(B - A) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Option (c) forgets to halve, (d) halves $A + B$, and (a) halves $A - B$.

questions.stem_md: Work out the product $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ -1 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}$.
questions.solution_md: Row by column: $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ -1 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \times 5 + 3 \times (-2) \\ (-1) \times 5 + 5 \times (-2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -15 \end{bmatrix}$. Option (d) multiplies the columns of the first matrix by the column, (a) has the wrong order (a $2 \times 2$ matrix times a $2 \times 1$ matrix gives a $2 \times 1$ matrix), and (b) ignores the minus sign of $-2$.

questions.stem_md: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, the matrix $A^2$ equals
questions.solution_md: $A^2 = A \times A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \times 1 + 3 \times 0 & 1 \times 3 + 3 \times (-1) \\ 0 \times 1 + (-1) \times 0 & 0 \times 3 + (-1) \times (-1) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, the identity matrix. Option (a) squares each element, and (b) is $2A$.

questions.stem_md: Let $A$ be any square matrix of order $2$ and $I$ the identity matrix of order $2$. Which statement is always true?
questions.solution_md: Multiplying by the identity matrix, on either side, leaves a matrix unchanged: $AI = IA = A$. The other statements fail for a matrix such as $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 5 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$.

questions.stem_md: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 \\ 3 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$, which statement about the products $AB$ and $BA$ is true?
questions.solution_md: $AB = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \times 3 + (-2) \times 3 & 2 \times 6 + (-2) \times 6 \\ 1 \times 3 + (-1) \times 3 & 1 \times 6 + (-1) \times 6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, but $BA = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \times 2 + 6 \times 1 & 3 \times (-2) + 6 \times (-1) \\ 3 \times 2 + 6 \times 1 & 3 \times (-2) + 6 \times (-1) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 12 & -12 \\ 12 & -12 \end{bmatrix}$. So $AB = O$ even though neither matrix is $O$, and $BA \ne O$.

questions.stem_md: Find $x$ if $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & x \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$.
questions.solution_md: The first row of the product is $3 \times 2 + x \times 1 = 6 + x$, so $6 + x = 10$ and $x = 4$. The second row checks: $-1 \times 2 + 2 \times 1 = 0$. Option (d) divides $10$ by $2$, and (a) adds $6$ instead of subtracting it.

questions.stem_md: What is $A^2$ when $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 3 \\ -3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$?
questions.solution_md: $A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \times 0 + 3 \times (-3) & 0 \times 3 + 3 \times 0 \\ (-3) \times 0 + 0 \times (-3) & (-3) \times 3 + 0 \times 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -9 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 \end{bmatrix}$, which is $-9I$. Option (a) loses the minus signs, and (b) squares each element.

questions.stem_md: Which matrix $X$ satisfies $A + X = O$, where $A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 8 \\ 0 & -5 \end{bmatrix}$ and $O$ is the zero matrix of order $2$?
questions.solution_md: $X = -A$: change the sign of every element of $A$. Option (b) is $A$ itself, (c) drops every minus sign instead of changing signs, and (d) is $O$.

questions.stem_md: $A$ is of order $1 \times 2$, $B$ is of order $2 \times 2$ and $C$ is of order $2 \times 1$. Which product is NOT defined?
questions.solution_md: $BA$ is not defined: $B$ has $2$ columns but $A$ has only $1$ row. $AB$ is $1 \times 2$, $BC$ is $2 \times 1$ and $AC$ is $1 \times 1$.

questions.stem_md: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ and $A^2 - 6A + kI = O$, find the number $k$.
questions.solution_md: $A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \times 4 + 1 \times (-1) & 4 \times 1 + 1 \times 2 \\ (-1) \times 4 + 2 \times (-1) & (-1) \times 1 + 2 \times 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 15 & 6 \\ -6 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ and $6A = \begin{bmatrix} 24 & 6 \\ -6 & 12 \end{bmatrix}$, so $A^2 - 6A = \begin{bmatrix} -9 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 \end{bmatrix} = -9I$. Then $-9I + kI = O$ gives $k = 9$. Option (d) forgets to move $-9I$ across.

questions.stem_md: Work out the product of the row matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$ and the square matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$, taken in that order.
questions.solution_md: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \times 3 + (-2) \times 4 & 1 \times 0 + (-2) \times 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -5 & -10 \end{bmatrix}$, a $1 \times 2$ matrix. Option (a) ignores the minus sign of $-2$, (b) has the wrong order, and (c) multiplies each row of the square matrix by one element.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** For $P = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ and any square matrix $Q$ of order $2$, $PQ = QP$.

**Reason (R):** Multiplication of matrices is commutative.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true: $P = 2I$, so $PQ = 2Q = QP$ for every $Q$. R is false: in general $AB \ne BA$; for example $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ but $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A matrix of order $2 \times 1$ cannot be added to a matrix of order $1 \times 2$.

**Reason (R):** Two matrices can be added only when they have the same order.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: R is the rule for addition, and the two orders in A are different, so A follows from R. Both are true and R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** If $A$ and $B$ are square matrices of order $2$ with $AB = O$, then $A = O$ or $B = O$.

**Reason (R):** The product of two non-zero matrices can be the zero matrix.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: R is true: $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ although neither matrix is $O$. That same example shows A is false.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The zero matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ is a square matrix.

**Reason (R):** Every element of a zero matrix is $0$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true because the matrix has as many rows as columns, $2$ each. R is also true, but having zero elements does not make a matrix square: $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ is a zero matrix of order $1 \times 2$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** If $2X = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -6 \\ 10 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, then $X = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

**Reason (R):** To multiply a matrix by a number, multiply every element by that number.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: It has $2$ rows of $2$ elements each: $2 \times 2 = 4$.

questions.solution_md: An identity matrix needs $1$ on the leading diagonal and $0$ elsewhere. $\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ is square but is not an identity matrix.

questions.stem_md: For any two square matrices $A$ and $B$ of order $2$, the products $AB$ and $BA$ are always equal.
questions.solution_md: Take $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$: $AB = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ but $BA = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$.

questions.stem_md: If $A$ and $B$ are both column matrices of order $2 \times 1$, then $A - B$ is also of order $2 \times 1$.
questions.solution_md: Subtraction works element by element on matrices of the same order, and the result keeps that order.

questions.stem_md: For all square matrices $A$ and $B$ of order $2$, $(A + B)^2 = A^2 + 2AB + B^2$.
questions.solution_md: $(A + B)^2 = A^2 + AB + BA + B^2$, which equals $A^2 + 2AB + B^2$ only when $AB = BA$. For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, $(A + B)^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ but $A^2 + 2AB + B^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$.

questions.solution_md: The column matrix has $1$ column but the square matrix has $2$ rows; these must be equal, so the product is not defined. (The other order, square matrix first, is defined.)

questions.stem_md: In the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -3 \\ 8 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, the element in the second row and first column is ___.
questions.solution_md: The second row is $8, 0$; its first element is $8$.

questions.stem_md: A matrix $P$ of order $1 \times 2$ is multiplied on the right by a matrix $Q$ of order $2 \times 2$. The order of $PQ$ is ___.
questions.solution_md: $P$ has $1$ row and $Q$ has $2$ columns, so $PQ$ is 1 × 2.

questions.solution_md: $2A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -2 \\ 10 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$, and $6 + (-2) + 10 + 4 = 18$.

questions.stem_md: For every square matrix $A$ of order $2$, the product of $A$ and the identity matrix $I$ of order $2$, in either order, equals ___.
questions.solution_md: The identity matrix leaves a matrix unchanged: AI = IA = A.

questions.solution_md: Row $1$ of the first matrix times column $2$ of the second: $2 \times (-1) + 5 \times 2 = 8$.

questions.stem_md: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, find the sum of the elements on the leading diagonal of $A^2$.
questions.solution_md: First-row, first-column element of $A^2$: $3 \times 3 + (-2) \times 1 = 7$. Second-row, second-column element: $1 \times (-2) + 1 \times 1 = -1$. Their sum is $7 + (-1) = 6$.

Equating corresponding elements: $x + 2y = 7$ (1) and $3x - y = 7$ (2).

From (2), $y = 3x - 7$. Substituting in (1): $x + 6x - 14 = 7$, so $7x = 21$ and $x = 3$.

questions.stem_md: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 5 \\ -2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$, evaluate $3A - 2B$.

questions.stem_md: Given $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, find $AB$ and $BA$. Is $AB = BA$?

answer.model_answer_md:
$AB = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \times 1 + 1 \times 4 & 2 \times (-1) + 1 \times 2 \\ 0 \times 1 + (-3) \times 4 & 0 \times (-1) + (-3) \times 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 0 \\ -12 & -6 \end{bmatrix}$.

$BA = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \times 2 + (-1) \times 0 & 1 \times 1 + (-1) \times (-3) \\ 4 \times 2 + 2 \times 0 & 4 \times 1 + 2 \times (-3) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 8 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$.

The corresponding elements differ (for example $6 \ne 2$ in the first place), so $AB \ne BA$: matrix multiplication is not commutative.

questions.stem_md: Find $x$ and $y$ if $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ 12 \end{bmatrix}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3x - 2y \\ x + 4y \end{bmatrix}$, so $3x - 2y = 8$ and $x + 4y = 12$.

Multiply the first equation by $2$ and add the second: $7x = 28$, so $x = 4$.

Then $4y = 12 - 4 = 8$, so $y = 2$.

questions.stem_md: Given $A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -1 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 7 \\ -4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, find the matrix $X$ for which $\dfrac{1}{2}X + A = B$.

questions.stem_md: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, show that $A^2 - 4A + I = O$, where $I$ is the identity matrix and $O$ the zero matrix of order $2$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \times 5 + (-2) \times 3 & 5 \times (-2) + (-2) \times (-1) \\ 3 \times 5 + (-1) \times 3 & 3 \times (-2) + (-1) \times (-1) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 19 & -8 \\ 12 & -5 \end{bmatrix}$.

$4A = \begin{bmatrix} 20 & -8 \\ 12 & -4 \end{bmatrix}$.

$A^2 - 4A + I = \begin{bmatrix} 19 - 20 + 1 & -8 + 8 + 0 \\ 12 - 12 + 0 & -5 + 4 + 1 \end{bmatrix}$

$= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = O$.

questions.stem_md: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Find the matrix $C$ such that $AB - C = 2A$.

answer.model_answer_md:

$2A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$.

From $AB - C = 2A$ we get $C = AB - 2A$.

$C = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 8 & 4 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 4 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$.

questions.stem_md: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, show that $(A + B)(A - B) \ne A^2 - B^2$, and explain why the identity from algebra fails for these matrices.

answer.model_answer_md:
$A + B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ and $A - B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$.

$(A + B)(A - B) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \times 2 + 0 \times (-2) & 2 \times (-2) + 0 \times (-2) \\ 4 \times 2 + 2 \times (-2) & 4 \times (-2) + 2 \times (-2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -4 \\ 4 & -12 \end{bmatrix}$.

$A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 6 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$, so $A^2 - B^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -4 \\ -4 & -8 \end{bmatrix}$, which is different.

Reason: $(A + B)(A - B) = A^2 - AB + BA - B^2$. Here $AB = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $BA = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 8 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$, so $BA - AB = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 8 & -4 \end{bmatrix} \ne O$, and this is exactly the difference between the two results.

questions.stem_md: Find $x$, $y$ and $z$ if $2\begin{bmatrix} x & 3 \\ -1 & y \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 4 & z \\ 6 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 8 \\ 4 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$.

Equating corresponding elements: $2x + 4 = 10$, so $x = 3$.

$6 + z = 8$, so $z = 2$.

$2y - 2 = 6$, so $y = 4$. The remaining elements agree: $-2 + 6 = 4$.

questions.stem_md: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$, find the numbers $p$ and $q$ for which $A^2 = pA + qI$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \times 3 + 2 \times 1 & 3 \times 2 + 2 \times 5 \\ 1 \times 3 + 5 \times 1 & 1 \times 2 + 5 \times 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 11 & 16 \\ 8 & 27 \end{bmatrix}$.

Equating elements: $2p = 16$ gives $p = 8$; then $3p + q = 11$ gives $q = 11 - 24 = -13$.

Check the other elements: $p = 8$ and $5p + q = 40 - 13 = 27$.

Answer each part.

(a) $A$ is of order $2 \times 2$, $B$ of order $2 \times 1$ and $C$ of order $1 \times 2$. Which of the products $AB$, $BA$, $CA$ and $AC$ are defined? Give the order of each product that is defined.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $AB$: $A$ has $2$ columns and $B$ has $2$ rows, so it is defined, of order $2 \times 1$. $BA$: $B$ has $1$ column but $A$ has $2$ rows, so it is not defined.

$CA$: $C$ has $2$ columns and $A$ has $2$ rows, so it is defined, of order $1 \times 2$. $AC$: $A$ has $2$ columns but $C$ has $1$ row, so it is not defined.

Then $\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \times 3 + 3 \times 2 \\ 2 \times 3 + (-1) \times 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 18 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$.

(b) If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -1 \\ 3 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, show that $A^2 - 3A = I$.

answer.model_answer_md:

So $2 + x = 7$, giving $x = 5$, and $y + 4 = 8$, giving $y = 4$. Check: $x - y = 5 - 4 = 1$.

(b) $A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \times 4 + (-1) \times 3 & 4 \times (-1) + (-1) \times (-1) \\ 3 \times 4 + (-1) \times 3 & 3 \times (-1) + (-1) \times (-1) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 13 & -3 \\ 9 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$.

$3A = \begin{bmatrix} 12 & -3 \\ 9 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$, so $A^2 - 3A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = I$.

(c) $Q + R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, so $P(Q + R) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \times 1 + (-1) \times 1 & 2 \times 3 + (-1) \times (-1) \\ 3 \times 1 + 2 \times 1 & 3 \times 3 + 2 \times (-1) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 7 \\ 5 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$.

$PQ = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 7 & -4 \end{bmatrix}$ and $PR = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 5 \\ -2 & 11 \end{bmatrix}$, so $PQ + PR = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 7 \\ 5 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$.

Hence $P(Q + R) = PQ + PR$.

(a) For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$, find $A + B$ and $A - B$, and verify that their sum is $2A$.

(b) Find $p$ and $q$ if $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} p \\ q \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 11 \end{bmatrix}$.

(c) For $P = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -6 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$ and $Q = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, find $PQ$ and $QP$. What do the results show about products of non-zero matrices, and about the order of multiplication?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $A + B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ and $A - B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -5 \\ 3 & -4 \end{bmatrix}$.

$(A + B) + (A - B) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -6 \\ 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, and $2A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -6 \\ 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, so the two are equal.

(b) Row by column: $3p + q = 6$ and $-p + 4q = 11$. From the first, $q = 6 - 3p$; then $-p + 24 - 12p = 11$, so $13p = 13$.

So $p = 1$ and $q = 6 - 3 = 3$.

(c) $PQ = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \times 4 + (-6) \times 2 & 3 \times 2 + (-6) \times 1 \\ 1 \times 4 + (-2) \times 2 & 1 \times 2 + (-2) \times 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, the zero matrix.

$QP = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \times 3 + 2 \times 1 & 4 \times (-6) + 2 \times (-2) \\ 2 \times 3 + 1 \times 1 & 2 \times (-6) + 1 \times (-2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 14 & -28 \\ 7 & -14 \end{bmatrix}$.

So the product of two non-zero matrices can be the zero matrix, and $PQ \ne QP$: the order of multiplication matters.

(b) If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $I$ is the identity matrix of order $2$, find $(A - 2I)(A + I)$.

(c) Find the $2 \times 2$ matrix $X$ such that $X \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 1 \\ 7 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Equating corresponding elements: $x - y = -1$ and $x + y = 7$. Adding, $2x = 6$, so $x = 3$; then $y = 7 - 3 = 4$.

(b) $A - 2I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ -2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $A + I = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 4 \\ -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.

$(A - 2I)(A + I) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \times 4 + 4 \times (-2) & 1 \times 4 + 4 \times 2 \\ (-2) \times 4 + (-1) \times (-2) & (-2) \times 4 + (-1) \times 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & 12 \\ -6 & -10 \end{bmatrix}$.

(c) Let $X = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$. Then $X \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a + 3b & b \\ c + 3d & d \end{bmatrix}$.

Equating with $\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 1 \\ 7 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$: $b = 1$ and $a + 3b = 5$, so $a = 2$; $d = 3$ and $c + 3d = 7$, so $c = -2$.

So $X = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$. Check: $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 1 \\ 7 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.

Answer each part.

(a) State the order of the product $\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 4 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ and evaluate it.

(b) If $B = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 4 \\ -2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, find $\dfrac{1}{2}B + 3I$, where $I$ is the identity matrix of order $2$.

(c) If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & x \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 9 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, find $x$. Hence show that $A^2 - 3A + 2I = O$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A $1 \times 2$ matrix times a $2 \times 2$ matrix is defined, and the product has order $1 \times 2$.

$\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 4 & -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \times 1 + (-2) \times 4 & 5 \times 3 + (-2) \times (-1) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 17 \end{bmatrix}$.

(b) $\dfrac{1}{2}B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $3I = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$, so $\dfrac{1}{2}B + 3I = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.

(c) $A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & x \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & x \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2x + x \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3x \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Comparing with $\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 9 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$: $3x = 9$, so $x = 3$.

With $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$: $3A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 9 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$, and $A^2 - 3A + 2I = \begin{bmatrix} 4 - 6 + 2 & 9 - 9 + 0 \\ 0 - 0 + 0 & 1 - 3 + 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = O$.

questions.stem_md:
Answer each part.

(a) Explain why the product $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$ is defined, state its order, and evaluate it.

(b) In an imagined inter-house quiz, a correct answer earns $4$ points and a wrong answer costs $1$ point. House Tagore gives $15$ correct and $5$ wrong answers; House Raman gives $12$ correct and $2$ wrong. Using $W = \begin{bmatrix} 15 & 5 \\ 12 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ and $S = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}$, find $WS$, and say which house leads and by how many points.

(c) If $A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 4 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ and $Y = 2A - 3I$, find $Y$ and show that $AY = YA$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The first matrix has $2$ columns and the second has $2$ rows, so the product is defined; its order is $2 \times 1$.

$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \times 1 + (-5) \times 3 \\ 0 \times 1 + 7 \times 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -13 \\ 21 \end{bmatrix}$.

(b) $WS = \begin{bmatrix} 15 \times 4 + 5 \times (-1) \\ 12 \times 4 + 2 \times (-1) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 55 \\ 46 \end{bmatrix}$.

House Tagore scores $55$ points and House Raman $46$, so Tagore leads by $55 - 46 = 9$ points.

(c) $Y = 2A - 3I = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 8 \\ 4 & 6 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 8 \\ 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.

$AY = \begin{bmatrix} (-1) \times (-5) + 4 \times 4 & (-1) \times 8 + 4 \times 3 \\ 2 \times (-5) + 3 \times 4 & 2 \times 8 + 3 \times 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 21 & 4 \\ 2 & 25 \end{bmatrix}$.

$YA = \begin{bmatrix} (-5) \times (-1) + 8 \times 2 & (-5) \times 4 + 8 \times 3 \\ 4 \times (-1) + 3 \times 2 & 4 \times 4 + 3 \times 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 21 & 4 \\ 2 & 25 \end{bmatrix}$, so $AY = YA$.
